title: Remediation SLA options + customer tier mapping (Hosted / Dedicated / Private) — working doc
text:
Doc purpose (Product Ops)
========================
We need a consistent set of internal remediation SLAs (time-to-mitigate / time-to-fix expectations) that:
- match what we can realistically execute across tiers (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)
- align with customer expectations and enterprise commitments (especially Dedicated/Private)
- can be implemented in tooling (ENG-4829 / SLA timers + breach alerts) without constant exceptions
- remains low-cardinality and understandable during live incidents

This is a working evaluation doc of options; final policy will live in Confluence in the Remediation SLA matrix.

Definitions
===========
- Remediation SLAs in this doc are internal operational targets and escalation triggers.
- We track two clocks:
  1) TTM (time-to-mitigate): time from incident declared (Sev assigned) to customer-impact mitigation in place (or credible workaround). Mitigation may include rollback, routing/fallback changes, traffic shaping, or isolating a bad region/model.
  2) TTF (time-to-fix): time from incident declared to a durable fix deployed OR a signed-off plan with committed ship date (depending on severity). For Sev0/Sev1, we typically expect a durable fix, not just a plan.

- “Tier” definitions:
  - Hosted: multi-tenant public API.
  - Dedicated: reserved capacity; stronger expectations for predictability and comms.
  - Private: VPC/on-prem control plane + data plane; sometimes customer-controlled networking and change windows.

- Severity (draft; matches on-call practice):
  - Sev0: broad outage / severe customer impact / safety risk / inability to serve core requests at scale.
  - Sev1: major degradation (e.g., high 5xx, severe latency) affecting meaningful customer set or a major enterprise customer; urgent.
  - Sev2: partial degradation; workarounds exist; limited scope.
  - Sev3: minor; limited impact; typically handled in normal on-call flow.

Decision principles
===================
1) Make the SLA actionable during incidents (what it forces us to do: staff, escalate, decide).
2) Keep differences by tier minimal, but acknowledge Dedicated/Private have different reality (capacity isolation, maintenance windows, customer networking).
3) Avoid a matrix so complex that incident-bot can’t enforce it.
4) “Pause/override” exists but must be auditable and rare.

Where tier differences are real (observations)
============================================
Hosted
- We control infra + routing + runtime deploys; can mitigate quickly via routing policies, throttles, or rollbacks.
- Customers accept “platform-wide” incidents but expect fast mitigation.

Dedicated
- Stronger expectations: named account pressure, high-touch comms, fewer acceptable repeated incidents.
- Mitigation sometimes means reallocating fleet capacity; can be constrained by GPU availability.
- Some mitigations require coordination with specific customer traffic patterns and agreed “degradation mode.”

Private
- Customer networking, DNS/TLS, firewalls, and change windows can dominate.
- “Mitigation” may require customer action; we can provide fix/instructions but can’t always execute.
- On-prem/air-gapped environments may block fast patching.

Key question: Do we set stricter SLAs for Dedicated/Private because customers pay more, or do we set realistic SLAs acknowledging dependencies and shift strictness into comms/escalation?

Option set
==========
Option A — Single SLA matrix (same targets across tiers) + comms escalation tiers
Pros: simple; consistent; easy to implement + dashboard.
Cons: risks being unrealistic for Private; breaches become noisy; forces frequent overrides.

Option B — Tier-adjusted TTF only (TTM consistent, TTF differs)
Pros: keeps the “stop the bleeding” behavior consistent; reflects reality that durable fixes take longer when customers control deploy windows.
Cons: still may be tight for certain Private classes; requires tier in SLA evaluator.

Option C — Tier-adjusted TTM and TTF (Dedicated stricter on TTM; Private looser on TTF)
Pros: matches customer expectation: Dedicated should be mitigated extremely fast; Private fixes can take longer.
Cons: more complex; risk of perceived unfairness (“why does private get longer?”).

Option D — Incident-type-aware SLA within severity (e.g., Private connectivity vs Control plane vs Runtime regression)
Pros: most accurate.
Cons: too complex for v1; high maintenance; taxonomy drift.

Recommendation (draft): Option B for v1
======================================
- Keep TTM targets consistent by severity across tiers (behavior we want in every incident: mitigate quickly).
- Allow tier-adjusted TTF targets (Private often needs customer maintenance window; Dedicated should still be fast but not necessarily faster than Hosted in all cases).
- In addition, define comms/escalation requirements by tier (Dedicated/Private proactive outreach thresholds), separate from remediation timers.

Proposed draft SLA targets (v1 candidate)
========================================
Notes:
- Times are proposed internal targets for breach alerting + leadership escalation.
- TTM measured to: restored SLO or reduced to acceptable degradation mode (documented).
- TTF measured to: fix deployed OR (Sev2/Sev3 only) fix scheduled with owner + date.

TTM (same across tiers)
-----------------------
Sev0: 30 minutes
Sev1: 2 hours
Sev2: 1 business day
Sev3: 5 business days (or next planned release train)

TTF (tier-adjusted)
-------------------
Hosted:
- Sev0: 24 hours
- Sev1: 3 business days
- Sev2: 10 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Dedicated:
- Sev0: 24 hours (same as Hosted; expectation is mitigation is faster, fix can be similar)
- Sev1: 5 business days (slightly longer than Hosted because some fixes involve fleet reshaping or customer-specific config review)
- Sev2: 15 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Private:
- Sev0: 48 hours (some fixes require customer coordination/change window; still want high urgency)
- Sev1: 10 business days
- Sev2: 20 business days
- Sev3: 45 business days

Rationale snapshots (to validate)
================================
- Private Sev0 TTF at 48h is the most controversial number. The intent is: if a Private incident is Sev0, we should be able to ship a fix quickly OR provide a validated workaround package quickly. But we may not be able to deploy it into the customer’s environment inside 48h. Proposed compromise: define “TTF = fix available” vs “TTF = deployed” for Private only.

Proposed adjustment for Private only:
- For Private tier: treat TTF as “fix available + customer delivery completed (artifact + instructions + support handoff)” rather than “fully deployed in customer environment.” Deployment tracking becomes a CS/Support deliverable.

This avoids constant SLA breaches from customer-controlled schedules, while still forcing Redwood to produce the fix quickly.

Edge cases + carve-outs (must be explicit)
=========================================
1) Cloud provider / upstream outage
- If root cause is confirmed upstream (AWS/GCP region/network, managed KMS outage, etc.):
  - TTM still applies (we should mitigate via failover/fallback where possible).
  - TTF may be waived or converted to “post-incident hardening actions” with due dates.
- Implementation requirement: incident-bot must allow “Upstream dependency” as a contributing factor and a “SLA exception reason” (audited).

2) Customer-caused or customer-controlled failures (mostly Private, occasionally Dedicated)
Examples:
- Customer rotated certs incorrectly; firewall blocks new endpoints; DNS misconfig; customer refuses recommended upgrade.
- TTM definition may be “workaround identified + communicated + support engaged.”
- TTF becomes a tracked action plan with customer owner and Redwood owner; SLA breach should not trigger paging.
- Implementation requirement: a controlled “Customer action required” exception reason.

3) Planned maintenance / change windows
- If incident is triggered by a planned change performed by Redwood:
  - SLAs still apply (we own it).
- If fix requires customer change window:
  - Private: allow “Fix available” measurement as above.

4) Multi-cause incidents
- Primary incident_type determines SLA class.
- Contributing systems recorded separately; do not create multiple SLA clocks.
- If reclassified, SLA clock should not reset (only severity changes reset behavior).

Comms and escalation requirements (separate from remediation timers)
===================================================================
We should not bake comms into remediation SLAs, but we do need consistent obligations by tier.

Draft comms rules (for CS alignment; see comms templates doc):
- Hosted
  - Sev0/Sev1: status page + initial update within 30 min; updates at least every 60 min until mitigated.
  - Sev2: case-by-case; internal update; status page optional.

- Dedicated
  - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach to affected accounts; initial customer-facing update within 30 min; updates every 60 min.
  - Sev2: proactive outreach within 1 business day if single account materially impacted.

- Private
  - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach; include “customer action required” assessment early.
  - Emphasize safe language: symptoms, mitigations, next update time.

Open issues / questions to resolve before signoff
=================================================
1) Private TTF definition: “available” vs “deployed”
- Need decision from SRE + Product Private (Vivek) + CS.

2) Dedicated Sev1 TTF: 3 vs 5 business days
- Dedicated product (Lauren) asked for realism: some changes require capacity rebalancing + canary.
- Counterpoint: enterprise expectation is faster. Maybe keep 3 BD but allow exceptions for capacity procurement work.

3) Severity-to-tier mapping clarity
- Can a Private incident be Sev0 if it affects only one customer? Yes, if it blocks core use case and is high urgency.
- Need crisp language in the incident process policy so on-call doesn’t under-severity enterprise incidents.

4) Implementation feasibility in tooling (ENG-4829)
- SLA evaluator needs tier + severity + type.
- Ensure we don’t create a combinatorial matrix. Proposed v1: severity x tier only, with optional overrides.

5) Reporting expectations
- Aisha to confirm dashboards will report:
  - SLA breach rate by tier, severity, incident_type
  - Exception counts by reason (upstream, customer-action, force majeure)

Data sanity check (informal)
============================
Based on last 2 quarters anecdotal review (see top-incidents analysis):
- Most Sev0/Sev1 mitigations happen within 15–90 minutes for Hosted when the mitigation is routing/rollback.
- Dedicated mitigations vary: quick when routing-only; slow when capacity constrained.
- Private “fix deployed” often exceeds 1–2 weeks due to customer windows; “fix available” is typically within a few days if we prioritize.

Action items (next steps)
=========================
- Rachel: circulate this doc to Rafael, Nikhil, Lauren, Vivek, Dev for comments (by 2026-02-07)
- Rafael/SRE: confirm if “TTF = plan w/ ship date” is acceptable for Sev2/Sev3 (Hosted/Dedicated) (by 2026-02-10)
- Vivek + CS: propose Private TTF measurement definition language for Confluence (by 2026-02-10)
- Lauren: confirm Dedicated Sev1 TTF target (3 vs 5 BD) and list top constraints (capacity procurement, release trains) (by 2026-02-12)
- Aisha: verify dashboards can label tier correctly and track exceptions without high cardinality (by 2026-02-12)

Appendix: quick matrix (for copy/paste)
======================================
TTM (all tiers):
- Sev0: 30m
- Sev1: 2h
- Sev2: 1 BD
- Sev3: 5 BD

TTF:
- Hosted:   Sev0 24h | Sev1 3 BD | Sev2 10 BD | Sev3 30 BD
- Dedicated:Sev0 24h | Sev1 5 BD | Sev2 15 BD | Sev3 30 BD
- Private:  Sev0 48h | Sev1 10 BD| Sev2 20 BD | Sev3 45 BD

Appendix: proposed SLA exception reasons (allowlist)
===================================================
- Upstream dependency confirmed (cloud/provider)
- Customer action required (customer-controlled environment)
- Force majeure (rare; requires Director+ approval)
- Mis-severity (initial severity incorrect; adjust and document)

(End)

title: Incident Ownership Mapping + Remediation SLA Matrix (v1)
text:
## Purpose
This page defines the **primary ownership mapping** for each incident type/subtype in the v1 taxonomy, plus **remediation SLAs** (time-to-mitigate and time-to-fix expectations) by **severity** and **customer tier** (Hosted / Dedicated / Private).

The intent is to:
- Make ownership **unambiguous** during live incidents (one accountable team per incident).
- Enable consistent paging/escalation and reporting by type/owner.
- Set realistic but improvement-driving remediation expectations.

**Applies to:** customer-impacting incidents and high-severity internal incidents that materially threaten reliability.

---

## Definitions (used throughout)
- **Primary owner:** the single team accountable for mitigation and driving the incident to resolution (may delegate tasks but retains accountability).
- **Secondary owner:** team likely needed for mitigation/fix; consulted early; may lead specific workstreams.
- **Consulted:** subject-matter experts who may be needed depending on symptoms.
- **Time-to-mitigate (TTM):** time from **incident declared** (Sev assigned) to a mitigation that restores service to within agreed SLO/SLA guardrails (or to “degraded but stable” per policy).
- **Time-to-fix (TTF):** time from **incident declared** to a durable fix (merged + deployed or config updated) that prevents recurrence of the same failure mode.

**Severity scale (v1):**
- **Sev0:** complete outage / widespread critical customer impact; no viable workaround.
- **Sev1:** major degradation (sustained 5xx/latency/streaming failures) affecting many customers or a top-tier Dedicated/Private tenant.
- **Sev2:** partial degradation or limited-scope impact; mitigations exist; some customers affected.
- **Sev3:** minor impact / near-miss / internal-only reliability risk.

---

## Escalation and paging rules (global)
1) **SRE is always paged for Sev0/Sev1** (IC + comms + coordination), regardless of incident type.
2) The **Primary owner on-call** is paged immediately once incident_type is set (or once the IC is confident on a likely type).
3) If incident_type is **Unknown/Unclassified** after 10 minutes:
   - IC pages **SRE + Platform Control Plane on-call** (default triage), then updates type as soon as evidence emerges.
4) **Multi-cause incidents:** pick a **single primary incident_type** based on the *first-order driver of customer impact* (see taxonomy decision tree). Record other drivers as **contributing systems** in the incident record/postmortem.
5) **Security triggers:** if auth failures look suspicious (credential stuffing, impossible travel, token anomalies) or audit findings require, **dual-track** with Security Ops (see security alignment page).
6) **Cloud provider / force majeure events:** still classify and mitigate, but SLA breach evaluation may be paused per the carve-outs section below.

**Escalation path (when primary owner cannot mitigate quickly):**
- **T+15 min (Sev0/1):** page secondary owner(s) if not already engaged.
- **T+30 min (Sev0/1):** page engineering manager (EM) for primary owner.
- **T+60 min (Sev0) / T+90 min (Sev1):** page director for primary owner; engage executive sponsor (SRE) if cross-org blockers persist.

---

## Ownership map (v1)
Notes:
- Team names align to current rotations and Slack channels.
- “Service boundary” indicates the system most likely to contain the change/fix.
- Owner mapping is implemented in control plane config (versioned + auditable) and consumed by incident-bot.

### Top-level incident types → ownership
| Incident type (v1) | Subtype (v1) | Primary owner (team) | Secondary owner(s) | Consulted | Primary service boundary | Primary Slack | Pager rotation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Availability / 5xx | Request 5xx spike (non-overload) | Platform Control Plane | Serving Runtime, Smart Routing | SRE, Observability | api-gateway, request-router, admission-control | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Availability / 5xx | Overload / admission control | Infrastructure/Fleet | Smart Routing | SRE, Observability, Runtime | fleet-manager, rate-limiters, batcher | #eng-infra-oncall | infra-fleet |
| Availability / 5xx | Dependency outage (DB/KV/queue) | Platform Control Plane | SRE | Observability | control-plane-db, config-store | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Latency regression | Global p95/p99 latency regression | Serving Runtime | Infrastructure/Fleet | SRE, Observability | runtime-scheduler, kernel-selector, batching | #eng-runtime-oncall | serving-runtime |
| Latency regression | Model rollout regression | Serving Runtime | SRE | Product, Observability | model-registry, rollout-controller | #eng-runtime-oncall | serving-runtime |
| Latency regression | Network path / cross-region latency | Infrastructure/Fleet | Private Deployments/Networking | SRE | edge-ingress, peering, region-network | #eng-infra-oncall | infra-fleet |
| Streaming | Stream disconnect spike | Platform Control Plane | Infrastructure/Fleet | Runtime, Support | streaming-gateway, websockets/sse layer | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Streaming | Partial tokens / stalled stream | Serving Runtime | Platform Control Plane | Observability | runtime-streamer, token-emitter | #eng-runtime-oncall | serving-runtime |
| Routing / fallback | Incorrect fallback policy execution | Smart Routing | Platform Control Plane | SRE, Observability | policy-engine, router | #eng-routing-oncall | smart-routing |
| Routing / fallback | Fallback loop / thrash | Smart Routing | Infrastructure/Fleet | Runtime, SRE | router, health-checker | #eng-routing-oncall | smart-routing |
| Routing / fallback | Region selection bug | Smart Routing | Infrastructure/Fleet | SRE | router, region-selector | #eng-routing-oncall | smart-routing |
| Capacity / fleet | Regional GPU shortage | Infrastructure/Fleet | Smart Routing | SRE, Support/CS | fleet-manager, provisioning | #eng-infra-oncall | infra-fleet |
| Capacity / fleet | Provisioning lag / autoscaler failure | Infrastructure/Fleet | Platform Control Plane | SRE | autoscaler, capacity-planner | #eng-infra-oncall | infra-fleet |
| Capacity / fleet | Dedicated tenant saturation | Infrastructure/Fleet | Support/CS | SRE, Product Dedicated | dedicated-scheduler, tenant-quotas | #eng-infra-oncall | infra-fleet |
| Control plane | Config write failures | Platform Control Plane | SRE | Observability, Support | control-plane-api, config-store | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Control plane | Rollout/registry outage | Platform Control Plane | Serving Runtime | SRE | model-registry, rollout-controller | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Auth / RBAC | Token issuance/validation failures | Security Ops | Platform Control Plane | SRE, Support | auth-service, api-gateway authn | #security-ops-oncall | security-ops |
| Auth / RBAC | RBAC/permission misconfig | Platform Control Plane | Security Ops | Support/CS | rbac-service, org-policy | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Telemetry / observability | Metrics ingestion outage | Observability | SRE | Platform, Runtime | metrics-pipeline, collectors | #eng-observability-oncall | observability |
| Telemetry / observability | Logging/tracing blind spot | Observability | Platform Control Plane | SRE | log-pipeline, trace-collector | #eng-observability-oncall | observability |
| Private deployments | Connectivity (DNS/TLS/VPN/peering) | Private Deployments/Networking | Infrastructure/Fleet | SRE, Support | private-gateway, customer-vpc-connect | #eng-private-oncall | private-networking |
| Private deployments | Customer config / upgrade regression | Private Deployments/Networking | Platform Control Plane | Support, SRE | private-agent, upgrade-controller | #eng-private-oncall | private-networking |

### Ownership notes for common disputed boundaries
**Overload vs routing:**
- If the *trigger* is lack of GPU capacity / saturation / provisioning lag → **Capacity/Fleet primary**.
- If the *trigger* is incorrect policy, routing loop, or wrong fallback execution even with healthy capacity → **Smart Routing primary**.
- If both present, choose the type that best explains the *first-order* customer impact and list the other as contributing.

**Streaming disconnects:**
- If disconnects correlate with gateway errors, websocket/SSE resets, or ingress churn → **Platform Control Plane primary**.
- If streams are established but stall mid-generation with runtime errors/oom/kv-cache thrash → **Serving Runtime primary**.

**Auth anomalies:**
- If it’s clearly a production bug (token validation library change, cert rotation mistake) → still classify under **Auth/RBAC**, but **Security Ops primary** unless Security explicitly delegates to Platform.

---

## Remediation SLA matrix (v1)
These are **internal remediation SLAs** used for operational discipline and reporting. Customer-facing SLA/credit terms remain governed by contracts and published policies.

### SLA philosophy by tier
- **Hosted:** optimize for fast mitigation; durable fixes follow normal change management unless Sev0/1.
- **Dedicated:** stronger expectation for mitigation + fix because customers have reserved capacity and explicit commitments.
- **Private:** mitigation may require customer participation; our SLA focuses on *our* response/mitigation within Redwood-managed components and clear handoffs.

### Default remediation SLAs by severity and tier
TTM and TTF are measured from the time the incident is declared with a severity.

| Severity | Hosted TTM | Hosted TTF | Dedicated TTM | Dedicated TTF | Private TTM | Private TTF |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sev0 | 30 min | 72 hours | 20 min | 48 hours | 30 min | 5 business days |
| Sev1 | 60 min | 5 business days | 45 min | 3 business days | 60 min | 10 business days |
| Sev2 | 4 hours | 10 business days | 3 hours | 7 business days | 4 hours | 15 business days |
| Sev3 | 2 business days | 30 days | 2 business days | 21 days | 3 business days | 45 days |

**Interpretation notes:**
- **TTM** = “service restored” or “degraded but stable” per incident commander + SRE sign-off.
- **TTF** requires a tracked change (PR/config) and deployment (or customer-delivered upgrade for Private, if the fix is on their side; see carve-outs).
- If a durable fix requires a longer roadmap change, the TTF can be met by delivering a **risk-reducing fix** (guardrail, rollback, safer default) plus a committed follow-up milestone.

### Type-specific adjustments (overrides)
Some incident types have different practical fix timelines. Use these overrides when applicable.

| Incident type | Subtype | Override applies to | Dedicated/Hosted/Private | TTF override | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|
| Control plane | Config write failures | Sev0–Sev2 | All | 3 business days | Config integrity bugs typically require code + migration; prioritize hotfix lane. |
| Telemetry / observability | Metrics ingestion outage | Sev0–Sev2 | All | 7 business days | Durable fix often includes capacity + pipeline changes; ensure interim mitigations (sampling, backpressure) are in place. |
| Private deployments | Connectivity (DNS/TLS/VPN/peering) | Sev0–Sev2 | Private | 10 business days | May require customer networking changes; our obligation is fast triage + clear “next action owner”. |
| Capacity / fleet | Regional GPU shortage | Sev0–Sev2 | Hosted/Dedicated | 10 business days | Durable fix may be procurement/provider constrained; require documented mitigation plan + capacity forecast update. |

**Who approves overrides:** SRE on-call for live incidents; post-incident, SRE program lead (Rafael Mendes) for reporting consistency.

---

## SLA timer start/stop + breach handling
### When the clock starts
- SLA clocks start when the incident is **declared** with severity (Sev0–Sev3) in incident-bot.
- If the incident is initially declared as Sev2 and later upgraded to Sev0/1, the SLA clock for that severity starts at the **upgrade time** (we retain the original for audit).

### When the clock stops
- **TTM stops** when mitigation is in place and validated via dashboards/metrics (or customer confirmation where metrics are unavailable).
- **TTF stops** when the fix is deployed (or config change is rolled out) and a verification check is complete.

### Pausing timers (allowed but audited)
Timers may be paused only with an explicit reason recorded in incident-bot:
- **Cloud provider outage / region-wide event** that is the dominant cause.
- **Customer-caused incident** (e.g., invalid client behavior, misconfigured private networking) once confirmed.
- **Force majeure** events.

**Pauses require:** SRE approval (Sev0/1) and a post-incident note describing evidence.

### Breach escalation
- Any projected TTM breach for **Sev0/Sev1** triggers:
  - Immediate page to primary owner EM at **T-10 min** to breach.
  - Escalation to director at breach time if not already engaged.
- Any actual breach triggers:
  - A postmortem requirement (Sev0/Sev1 always; Sev2 if breach is customer-impacting).
  - A follow-up ticket tagged **reliability-sla-breach** with owner + due date.

---

## How to use this during an incident (operator checklist)
1) Declare incident + set severity.
2) Classify **incident_type/subtype** using the decision tree.
3) Confirm **Primary owner** from mapping (incident-bot will resolve after selection).
4) Page primary owner on-call; add secondary owners if the boundary is unclear.
5) Track TTM and TTF targets in the incident channel topic (incident-bot prints due times).
6) If classification changes, update incident_type and record the reason.

---

## Examples
### Example A: Dedicated tenant sees 429s during burst
- Symptoms: 429s + queue depth + GPU utilization pinned.
- Classification: **Capacity / fleet → Dedicated tenant saturation**.
- Primary owner: **Infrastructure/Fleet**.
- Secondary: **Support/CS** (customer comms + burst expectations).
- SLA (Dedicated Sev1 typical): **TTM 45 min, TTF 3 business days**.

### Example B: Global spike in streaming disconnects after gateway deploy
- Symptoms: websocket resets, elevated gateway errors, runtime healthy.
- Classification: **Streaming → Stream disconnect spike**.
- Primary owner: **Platform Control Plane**.
- SLA (Hosted Sev1 typical): **TTM 60 min, TTF 5 business days**.

### Example C: Auth failures with suspicious pattern
- Symptoms: token validation failures, anomalous IP patterns.
- Classification: **Auth / RBAC → Token issuance/validation failures**.
- Primary owner: **Security Ops** (dual-track security incident if warranted).

---

## Changelog
- **2026-02-12:** Clarified overload vs routing primary-owner rule; added TTF override for regional GPU shortage; added timer pause requirements.
- **2026-01-24:** Added Private connectivity subtype details and clarified customer handoff expectations.
- **2026-01-10:** Initial v1 published.

title: incidents
text:
incident-bot: :rotating_light: SEV2 Paging — SmartRouting detected unstable fallback loop for customer="LedgerCo" in region=eu-central-1. Elevated 5xx and latency spikes since 02:12 UTC. Pager to oncall.

maria: oncall here. assigning to oliver for initial triage. @oliver can you take?

oliver: taking. quick summary pls — is this policy-engine level or runner errors?

sam: logs show alternating decisions: policy marks quant variant as incompatible for tool-calls, routes to fp16 in us-west-2, remote rejects because of context_limit mismatch, then policy tries original again. loop period ~15s per session.

rachel-cs: LedgerCo has flagged failed payments calls and webhook timeouts. They've throttled some traffic but still seeing errors. Requesting ETA and status.

oliver: priority: (A) break loop, (B) reduce customer impact, (C) find root cause. Proposing immediate disable of cross-region fallback for LedgerCo via policy override.

maria: agree. oliver, can you flip a customer-scoped rule quickly?

oliver: executing emergency toggle: `POST /console/policies/overrides` body: `{ "customer": "ledgerco", "fallback": false }`

deploy-bot: rollout started: policy-override/ledgerco-no-fallback/2178976543

monitoring-bot: smart-routing.loop-rate[ledgerco]=70 -> 3 (post-toggle), median_p95_latency=1.8s -> 240ms

oliver: loop rate dropped immediately. good. we'll keep fallback disabled while debugging.

sam: digging into model compatibility records — looking at model-compat-table entries for `redwood-6b-q4` (quant) and `redwood-6b-fp16`.

sam: found entry: `redwood-6b-q4: { tool_call_support: false, max_context: 4096 }` but actual manifest for deployed quant binary indicates `tool_call: true` and `max_context: 8192`.

oliver: so onboarding metadata is wrong. policy thinks quant can't do tool calling => forces fallback to fp16 in other region.

sam: exact error trace from policy-engine: `CompatCheckError(variant=redwood-6b-q4, missing=tool_call) -> choose variant=redwood-6b-fp16@us-west-2 -> RemoteError(incompatible_context)`. Loop repeats.

rachel-cs: LedgerCo impact: spike in failed transactions, some duplicate requests visible. They've requested postmortem and will need timeline.

maria: immediate mitigations: (1) keep customer fallback disabled, (2) patch compat-table entry to reflect true capabilities, (3) invalidate policy-engine cache. We'll stage changes carefully.

oliver: applying compat-table patch now via models-api: `PATCH /models/compat/redwood-6b-q4` payload: `{ "tool_call_support": true, "max_context": 8192 }`

deploy-bot: models-api/compat-patch started: job=patch-7711

deploy-bot: models-api/compat-patch succeeded: job=patch-7711

sam: cache invalidation request to policy-engine: `POST /policy/cache/invalidate?model=redwood-6b-q4` -> acknowledged.

monitoring-bot: policy-compat-check.failures[ledgerco] -> 0; smart-routing.loop-rate -> 0; p95 latency -> 210ms

oliver: canary plan: keep override for 10m, then enable fallback for 2% sessions, ramp to 25% if stable. Maria, can you coordinate the canary?

maria: starting canary at 02:38 UTC with 2%.

monitoring-bot: ledgerco-route-health: error_rate 0.3% (pre-mitig 5.1%), median_latency 220ms

title: SLO Launch Field Kit and Ops Liaison Rotations
text:
Purpose and scope:

This is a compact field kit for launching service-level objectives (SLOs) across teams and for establishing a temporary ops liaison rotation to smooth the first 60–90 days of a rollout. Focus is cross-functional: product/feature teams, platform, SRE, and solutions eng. Use this doc as a checklist + working notes during the pilot phase of any new SLO or major SLO change.

Why this is needed (problem statement):
- SLO launches often stall because operational responsibilities are not clear in the first weeks; telemetry thresholds, alerts, and stakeholder triggers are misaligned.
- Early false positives and noisy alerts erode trust; teams revert or mute signals before the SLO has time to stabilize.
- There is no lightweight, repeatable rotation pattern for platform to support feature teams during the critical onramp.

High-level goals (success criteria):
1) First 30 days: no critical outages caused by misconfigured SLO alerts and a documented runbook for common alarms.
2) 60 days: measured signal quality (false positive rate < 20% for new alerts) and adoption of at least one mitigation automation (auto-scaling, fallback routing, or pre-warm).
3) 90 days: handoff complete, liaison exits rotation, and SLO is owned by product + SRE with an agreed cadence for review.

Who should be involved (roles & responsibilities):
- Feature/Product Owner: defines customer-facing intent, key user journeys, and impact matrix.
- SRE Lead (onboarded): owns alert tuning, runbook creation, and postmortem process.
- Platform Engineer Liaison (rotation): provides immediate help on routing, capacity and config; bridges to infra teams.
- Observability Engineer: sets up telemetry, dashboards, and synthetic probes.
- Solutions/SE contact: validates customer-facing behavior and rollout comms.
- QA / Perf: runs spike tests and validates thresholds under load.

Ops liaison rotation pattern (recommended):
- Length: 2-week stints for each liaison, 8–12 weeks total support window for a typical SLO launch.
- Roster: platform-engineering contributors + 1 SRE buddy per sprint. Minimum overlap: 3 days handoff between liaisons.
- On-call parity: liaisons should not replace primary oncall but act as subject-matter responders for SLO-specific signals.
- Deliverables per liaison period: updated runbook section, 1 tuning pass on alerts, one dashboard iteration, and a documented de-noising action (e.g., metric filter, composite alert).

Launch checklist (pre-launch, day 0, week 1–4, week 5–12):
A) Pre-launch (2–4 weeks before):
- Confirm intent doc and customer journeys (owner: Product).
- Define measurable SLOs, indicators (SLIs), and error budgets (owner: SRE + Product).
- Create initial dashboards and synthetic checks (owner: Observability).
- Draft runbook template with triage steps and tests to reproduce (owner: Feature + SRE).
- Map linked artifacts (Jira tickets, PRs, Confluence pages) and communication list.
- Identify liaison roster and confirm rotation schedule.

B) Day 0 (go-live):
- Smoke test synthetic checks and baseline dashboards.
- Turn on alerts in quiet mode (notify-only) for 24–48 hours if possible.
- Liaison kickoff sync (15–30m): align handoff, urgent contacts, quick war-room plan.

C) Week 1–2 (stabilize):
- Triage initial alerts, categorize noise vs real incidents.
- Runbook iteration 1: codify observed triage patterns.
- Quick perf stress: run narrow spike tests during low-traffic window.
- Postmortem-lite for any incidents (owner: SRE + Feature).

D) Week 3–4 (de-noise):
- Tune alert thresholds and apply suppression windows where appropriate.
- Instrument additional SLIs if gaps are identified.
- Begin scheduling regular SLO review slots (biweekly for first 8 weeks).

E) Week 5–12 (handoff & automation):
- Implement at least one automation (auto-scaling profile, warm pool, or fallback).
- Validate that false positive rate trends downward and alert precision improves.
- Formal handoff doc completed and accepted by SRE + Product.
- Liaison rotation concludes once ownership sign-off is obtained.

Key artifacts and templates (starter snippets to copy):
- Runbook template: Summary, who to page, triage steps, mitigations, escalation, reversion plan, postmortem link.
- Tuning log: timestamped entries of alert parameter changes and rationale.
- Signal health spreadsheet: counts of alerts, incidents, false positives, mean time to acknowledge, mean time to mitigate.
- Handoff acceptance checklist: runbook complete, dashboards stable, automation validated, errors within agreed budget.

Signal quality metrics to track (minimum set):
- Alert volume / day (broken down by severity).
- False positive rate (manual classification during liaison period).
- Time to acknowledge (TTA) and time to mitigate (TTM).
- Error budget consumption trajectory (7-day and 30-day).
- User-facing impact incidents (severity >= P2) during onramp.

Common early risks and mitigations: 
- Risk: Noisy client-side retries inflate error rate. Mitigation: add client-side dedupe or sampling, instrumented counts for retries.
- Risk: Misaligned aggregation windows causing spike sensitivity. Mitigation: align SLI windows with user-visible latency patterns; test with synthetic traffic.
- Risk: Runbook absent or incomplete. Mitigation: liaison must publish a minimally viable runbook in first 72 hours.

Communication plan (who/when/how):
- Pre-launch email to stakeholders summarizing intent and schedule.
- Day 0 status Slack channel with pinned runbook and contacts.
- Weekly short “signal health” bulletin during liaison rotation (2–3 bullet summary).
- Post-launch retrospective at day 30 and day 90.

Decision gates for rollback or pause:
- If error budget consumption > 50% within first 7 days and user-impacting incidents occur -> pause rollout and invoke rollback plan.
- If alert false positive rate > 50% after week 2 -> escalate to SRE lead and schedule immediate tuning block.

Handoff acceptance criteria (to exit liaison rotation):
- Runbook passes checklist and is accessible to the oncall team.
- False positives reduced to under 20% for key alerts or clear mitigation path documented.
- Observability baseline established (synthetics, dashboards, and alerting stable for 7 consecutive days).
- Product and SRE sign off on continued cadence and review frequency.

Quick templates (copy into a new doc):
- Liaison handoff note: dates, current open actions, known flakes, critical dashboards, next steps.
- Runbook snippet: Immediate mitigation -> Scale up warm pool; If warm pool insufficient -> reroute traffic to fallback model; If user-impacting -> page SRE lead.

Open questions / decisions pending (working):
1) Do we require all SLO launches to run liaison rotations by policy, or keep as recommended? (proposal: recommended for first 3 months after rollout)
2) What is the minimal data retention for signal tuning logs? (proposal: 90 days)
3) Who owns the liaison roster and backfill commitments across holidays? (proposal: platform-engineering to maintain primary roster, SRE to provide secondary coverage)

Next steps (immediate owner assignments):
- Evelyn (owner): finalize roster and publish calendar invites for next pilot (by 2026-05-18).
- Diego (Observability): create the synthetic checks template and baseline dashboard (by 2026-05-20).
- Priya (SRE): draft runbook template and postmortem-lite checklist (by 2026-05-21).

Notes to self / tacit knowledge:
- Keep liaison tasks lightweight — do the minimal set of changes that restore signal fidelity without overengineering.
- Communicate progress with short bullets; engineers stop reading long prose during active incidents.
- Preserve a short tuning history for auditability; teams will ask why thresholds moved.

If you use this kit: copy the runbook template, fill the liaison roster, and reach out in #platform-slo-onramp with questions or to request help.

Document history: initial draft 2026-05-12 by Evelyn Park; liaison pattern suggestions and checklist edits added 2026-06-03 by Diego Ramos and Priya Nair.

title: incidents
text:
sre_bot: :rotating_light: INCIDENT alert - production canary cluster latency regressions detected after the 1792123000 deploy. Threshold breach: p95 latency > 1200ms on text-gen route. Auto-paging to #incidents.

emma_oncall: I’m on it. joining call in 2. Any immediate customer-facing impact?

ben_customer_ops: Seeing 5 support tickets from two customers (acme-corp, healthlytics) complaining about timeouts in doc-summarize flow. Not widespread, but important for SLAs.

raj_runtime: Observing kernel fallback logs on several canary pods. Root cause looks like new batching changes pushing memory usage -> OOM-triggered fallback to slow kernel path. Repro: high-concurrency + long context.

olivia_prod: @emma_oncall please confirm whether we can flip the feature-flag for the new batching algorithm. There's a kill-switch in config service.

emma_oncall: Pulling kill-switch now. Calling out steps in case rollback needed.

emma_oncall: RUNNING now: 
```
# flip kill-switch via admin API
curl -XPOST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  https://config.redwood-inference.internal/api/v1/flags/batching_v2/disable
```

emma_oncall: Flag flip submitted, waiting for propagation (30s).

devops_bot: Feature-flag update event received. Propagation to canary region completed.

raj_runtime: Confirming metrics: p95 dropped from ~1300ms to ~420ms over the last 60s after flag flip. Kernel fallback logs decreasing. Memory used on canary nodes trending down.

ben_customer_ops: Reopened one ticket and updated customers: "We've rolled back a recent batching change and are monitoring; ETA 10-15m". They acknowledged.

emma_oncall: Good. However load test shows a handful of canary pods still intermittently falling back to fallback-kernel under synthetic stress. I'm going to trigger a canary rollback of the release to be safe. Rolling back via deploy bot.

emma_oncall: /deploy rollback --release 1792123000 --canary-only

devops_bot: Deploy rollback started for release 1792123000 (canary). Step 1/3: stop new pods. Step 2/3: start previous release image.

raj_runtime: While rollback proceeds, I'm going to disable continuous-batching on runtime node config to avoid queue buildup which exacerbates fallback. Small config tweak: set batching.max_batch_size=32, batching.max_wait_ms=20.

emma_oncall: Apply command snippet: 
```
# kubectl patch configmap runtime-config -n canary --type merge -p '{"data":{"batching.max_batch_size":"32","batching.max_wait_ms":"20"}}'
```

raj_runtime: Patch applied. Observability: queue depth back to normal, no more OOM events in logs.

devops_bot: Rollback to previous image completed on 6/6 canary pods. Health checks passing.

olivia_prod: Assigning post-incident ticket to runtime and release engineering to do root-cause analysis and tighten canary criteria. Jordan, can you own customer comms follow-up?

jordan_pm: Yep, I'll draft a note and coordinate with Ben for affected customers. We'll include mitigation and next steps.

emma_oncall: Handoff: I'm going to run a diagnostic sweep for 15m, then hand to @olivia_prod for overnight monitoring. Current status: mitigation successful, rollback completed, customer impact limited and acknowledged.

olivia_prod: Taking over monitoring. Please leave notes in the incident doc: link to logs, commands, and timeline.

raj_runtime: Quick log snippets for RCA: 
```
# observed stack traces
2028-07-21T14:12:03Z runtime ERROR kv_cache: eviction triggered, mem_used=89% -> kernel_fallback
2028-07-21T14:12:04Z runtime WARN batching: queue_depth=120, max_batch_size=256, wait_ms=200
```

raj_runtime: Hypothesis: new batching_v2 increases max_batch_size and wait_ms for throughput improvements; under certain concurrency patterns this pushes memory pressure which trips kernel safety fallback. Fallback path currently ~3-4x slower.

emma_oncall: Next actions (assigned):
- raj_runtime: run targeted load tests to reproduce and tune batching parameters, consider adaptive limits.
- eng-runtime: add guardrails to disable batching_v2 automatically when mem > 80% on canary.
- release_eng: review deploy gating to include memory/fallback smoke checks in canary.
- jordan_pm + ben_customer_ops: follow up comms.

ben_customer_ops: I'll keep open tickets updated and close once customers confirm stable.

devops_bot: Incident severity downgraded to P2. Time to mitigation: ~9 minutes from page.

emma_oncall: Closing thread for active mitigation, keeping incident doc open for RCA write-up. Thanks everyone. :thumbsup:

olivia_prod: Acknowledged. Taking 1hr monitoring shift now.
